w: What's tested The numbers and hallmarks his objectives name: 20 percent blasts for most AML, what blasts and Auer rods mean, and how acute and chronic leukemia differ in the clinic and on the blood count Acute promyelocytic leukemia (abnormal promyelocytes, t(15;17) and PML-RARA, the risk of DIC, all-trans retinoic acid with arsenic trioxide) and chronic myeloid leukemia (the Philadelphia chromosome, its phases, its blood count, imatinib) Lymphoma basics: why it needs a tissue sample and how the specimen is sent, what flow cytometry does, the B symptoms, and how Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma present differently Each lymphoma's defining cell, translocation or infection: CLL/SLL's smudge cells, follicular t(14;18), mantle cell t(11;14), MALT lymphoma and H. pylori, DLBCL, Burkitt's t(8;14) and EBV, Reed-Sternberg cells, plasmacytoma versus myeloma, and the T-cell lymphomas What shows in the mouth and the head and neck: swollen gums from AML in the gingiva, the endemic Burkitt jaw, the hard palate destroyed by extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, a salivary MALT lymphoma after Sjögren syndrome, bleeding gums from low platelets His objectives say you don't need the individual markers on the slides (CD20, CD5, CD34 and the rest) Dr. Sam Borak gives Lecture 20 on Tuesday, November 17, at 2 pm. His deck, "Lymphoma/Leukemia", starts with how blood cells mature and how a lymphoma is diagnosed, covers leukemia in general and the bone marrow exam, walks through the major lymphomas one at a time, and ends with chronic myeloid leukemia and the acute leukemias. These notes are from the slides; the lecture is Tuesday, and they will be checked against its recording. His two objectives slides are the best guide to the exam: nearly every disease below has its own objective. Both say you don't need the individual markers (CD20, CD5, CD34, CD117, CD3 and the rest), and the leukemia slide adds that you don't need every type of acute leukemia, only the ones he discusses. How blood cells mature All blood cells come from the hematopoietic stem cell in the marrow, which can renew itself or differentiate. It gives rise to two lines: the myeloid line (red cells, platelets, granulocytes such as neutrophils, and monocytes) and the lymphoid line (B cells, T cells and NK cells). Leukemias and lymphomas are cancers of these cells, and each tends to look like, and carry the markers of, the normal cell it comes from. The neutrophil line matures in a fixed order, and his objectives ask for it: myeloblast, promyelocyte, myelocyte, metamyelocyte, band, and finally the segmented neutrophil, or PMN. The blast is the youngest cell. Acute leukemia is a disease of blasts; chronic myeloid leukemia fills the blood with the later, maturing stages; and in acute promyelocytic leukemia, maturation stops at the promyelocyte. The lymphatic system and what a lymphoma is The lymphatic system is the lymphatic vessels, the lymph nodes, the lymphoid organs, lymphatic tissue and the lymph itself. It produces immune cells and removes excess fluid from the body. A lymphoma is a blood cancer that starts in the lymphatic system and affects the lymphocytes, the white cells at the center of the immune system. The key practical point: the diagnosis requires sampling of tissue, such as a lymph node or the bone marrow. A blood count or a scan can raise the suspicion, but the tissue makes the diagnosis. (CLL, which lives in the blood, is the one he teaches that is diagnosed from a blood count.) The B symptoms His slide on the general signs and symptoms of lymphoma is a picture; the three symptoms he spells out have their own name, the B symptoms: A fever of 38 degrees Celsius or higher with no obvious cause Night sweats that soak the bedding and clothes Unexplained weight loss of at least 10 percent of body weight over the past 6 months Watch how often each lymphoma brings them: B symptoms are uncommon in follicular lymphoma and rare in MALT lymphoma; DLBCL can bring them, and peripheral T-cell lymphoma usually does; and in classic Hodgkin lymphoma they appear in about 20 percent of localized and 70 percent of advanced disease. The tissue: H and E, immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry His slides set a normal lymph node, with its follicles, beside a pathologic node, whose architecture is replaced, or effaced, by tumor cells. The lab reads the tissue three ways: the routine H and E stain for morphology; immunohistochemistry, antibodies that stain proteins in the section; and flow cytometry, which reads living cells one at a time in suspension. That is why the specimen handling matters. When you collect the specimen, don't put it in formalin: formalin fixes the cells, and flow cytometry needs them fresh. It may need a special medium, such as RPMI or Hanks's solution. Flow cytometry detects proteins on the cell membrane, the cell surface markers, with polyclonal or monoclonal antibodies stained by an immunofluorescent method. A laser passes through each cell, and the scattered light tells two things: forward (low-angle) scatter indicates the cell's volume or size, and side scatter estimates its complexity or granularity. A granular cell such as a promyelocyte scatters a lot of light to the side; a small lymphocyte scatters little either way. His slide groups the markers into myeloid (CD13, CD33, CD117, MPO), B-lymphoid (CD10, CD19, CD22, CD79a) and T-lymphoid (CD2, CD3, CD5, CD7, CD4, CD8). His objectives say you don't need the individual markers, so no question asks for one. What to know is the idea: a lymphoma or leukemia carries the markers of the normal cell it comes from, so flow cytometry and immunohistochemistry show its lineage. Classifying lymphoma Lymphoma is classified on many parameters together: the clinical presentation, imaging, and a range of laboratory tests. No single test decides it, although morphology remains the key component, with immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry playing a major role. B-cell and T-cell lymphomas resemble the normal B and T cells they arise from, which is what lets the stains sort them. The slides follow the World Health Organization classification. The vast majority of lymphoid neoplasms, 85 to 90 percent, are of B-cell origin. The rest are T-cell neoplasms, and tumors of NK-cell origin are rare. Lymphoma in the eye, the head and neck, and the mouth Lymphoma can arise outside the nodes, and his slides show several sites near your work. Ocular adnexal lymphoma involves the orbit, eyelids, conjunctiva, lacrimal gland or lacrimal sac. Inside the eye there is vitreoretinal and uveal lymphoma. These cause a painless decrease in vision or floaters; patients without symptoms are often found on eye screening; and when the brain is involved, personality changes are a common first sign. In the head and neck, lymphoma can involve the tonsils (part of Waldeyer ring, the ring of lymphoid tissue around the throat), and the oral mucosa and gums; his slides set normal tissue beside tissue taken over by lymphoma, and cite a study of oral lymphomas in people with and without HIV. Staging His slide shows the Ann Arbor staging system as a chart. In the standard system, stage I is one lymph node region; stage II is two or more regions on the same side of the diaphragm; stage III is nodes on both sides of the diaphragm; and stage IV is widespread involvement of organs outside the lymphatic system, such as the bone marrow or liver. The letter B after a stage means the patient has B symptoms, and A means none. The staging slide is a picture, so the stages above are the standard Ann Arbor chart (Robbins) rather than words from his slide; no question here depends on them. What leukemia is Leukemia is a malignant disease of the hematopoietic tissue in which neoplastic blood cells replace the normal bone marrow and peripheral blood elements. The neoplastic cells are usually white cells; less common variants involve the red cell (erythroid) or platelet (megakaryocyte) lines. Leukemia frequently starts in the bone marrow and can extend to the reticuloendothelial system (the spleen, liver and lymph nodes) and to other tissues. Untreated, it is fatal. Its clinical features come two ways. Marrow failure, as the leukemic cells crowd out normal blood-making: anemia, with fatigue, malaise and pallor; bruising and bleeding from too few platelets; and fever and infections from too few working white cells. Organ infiltration, as the leukemic cells grow in tissues: bone and joint pain from the expanding marrow; splenomegaly, hepatomegaly and lymphadenopathy; neurologic symptoms; and gingival hypertrophy and oral lesions. For the dentist, both sides show in the mouth: pale mucosa, bleeding gums and petechiae from marrow failure, and swollen gums from leukemic cells growing in them. The swollen gums of acute monocytic leukemia come up again near the end of the lecture. The bone marrow exam Leukemia is diagnosed from the blood smear and the bone marrow. The marrow is sampled two ways, usually at one sitting: an aspirate, liquid marrow drawn through a needle and smeared on slides to read the individual cells, and a core biopsy, a small cylinder of bone and marrow that shows the marrow's structure and how cellular it is. Posterior iliac crest Biopsy and aspirate Sternum Aspirate only Tibia Aspirate only, in small children One marrow exam fills a folder of slides: a peripheral blood smear, "crush" and "push" marrow smears, a touch imprint of the core, a clot section of the aspirated particles, and the core biopsy. Acute versus chronic leukemia His two comparison slides set acute leukemia beside chronic leukemia; his chronic column is chronic myeloid leukemia. Who Usually children and the young Usually middle-aged and older Onset Rapid Insidious Course if untreated Less than 6 months 2 to 6 years Cells Immature cells: blasts Mature cells Blasts More than 20 (up to 95) percent of the marrow; more than 5 (up to 95) percent of the blood Fewer than 20 percent, in marrow and blood White count Usually increased, from the blasts, but variable Increased Anemia Mild to severe Mild Platelets Low to very low Normal to increased early, then decreased Organs Mild organomegaly Prominent organomegaly Treatment Chemotherapy, bone marrow transplant Chemotherapy, possibly a transplant Death Infection or bleeding Infection or bleeding Diagnosis Blood smear, marrow exam, stains, flow cytometry, cytogenetics Blood smear, marrow, cytogenetics (the Philadelphia chromosome) The thread through it: acute leukemia is blasts that don't mature, filling the marrow fast, so the other lines fail fast; chronic leukemia is cells that still mature, so the count climbs slowly, the spleen and liver fill up, and the platelets hold up until late. His acute column says "usually children and the young", but his AML slide gives AML a median age of 65 and calls it common in adults. Both hold: ALL is the acute leukemia of young children, and AML is the acute leukemia of older adults. If a question asks who gets AML, it is adults. Classifying the acute leukemias There are two broad categories of acute leukemia. Acute myeloid leukemia (AML). The older system split it into subtypes M0 through M7 by the type of cell differentiation; the WHO now classifies some types by their common genetic abnormalities. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). The WHO divides it by genetic abnormality, and into precursor B-cell (B-ALL) and T-cell (T-ALL) types. The number his objectives ask for is the blast threshold. For the AML types defined by a genetic abnormality, "you can diagnose AML no matter blast count". For the others, the blasts must be over 20 percent, the threshold his objectives call the one for diagnosing most AML. Fewer blasts than that, in a patient with abnormal counts, point to something else, such as a myelodysplastic syndrome (later in these notes). His slide writes the threshold as "greater than 20 percent"; the WHO wording is 20 percent or more. Either way, the number to know is 20. Who Common in adults (median age 65); relatively rare in children Common in children: highest at 1 to 5 years, peak at 2 to 3; poor prognosis under 1 year; less common in adults Blood Anemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia; myeloblasts (20 to 95 percent) Anemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia; lymphoblasts Blast size Medium to large, high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio Small to medium Cytoplasm Moderate, with granules, and Auer rods Scant, no granules Nucleus Fine chromatin, distinct nucleoli Fine chromatin, indistinct nucleoli Outside the marrow Spleen, liver (lymph nodes, CNS) Nodes, spleen, liver, CNS, gonads Marrow Myeloid-to-erythroid ratio usually high Not on his slide Auer rods Can be present Never: Auer rods exclude ALL The rule that settles a smear: Auer rods exclude ALL. Find one, and the blast is myeloid. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia and small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL) CLL/SLL is a lymphoma of small, mature B cells. It is one disease with two names, depending on where it is. CLL is diagnosed from the blood: a B-cell count of at least 5 times 10 to the 9th per liter (5,000 per microliter), with the typical look and markers. SLL is diagnosed from tissue: an enlarged organ, such as a lymph node over 15 millimeters, infiltrated by the same cells, with fewer than 5 times 10 to the 9th circulating B cells per liter. Who and how: the median age at diagnosis is 70 or older, and a family history of CLL is a risk factor. It may cause no symptoms at first and be found only by a lymphocytosis on a routine count, or by enlarged nodes or spleen. When it does cause symptoms, they are cytopenias (anemia, low platelets and, rarely, low neutrophils, from marrow infiltration or from autoimmune destruction), recurrent infections, lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly. The infections come from hypogammaglobulinemia, too little normal antibody, and from defective cellular immunity. The look, which his objective stresses "particularly in blood": small lymphocytes with clumped chromatin, a pattern compared to cracked mud or a soccer ball, and many smudge cells, fragile lymphocytes crushed flat as the smear is made. In the marrow the involvement can be nodular, interstitial, diffuse, or a mix. In a lymph node the small cells infiltrate diffusely, with pale areas of larger cells called proliferation centers. Its course: despite much better outcomes since targeted therapies arrived, CLL/SLL remains largely incurable, with a slow but progressive course. The markers on his CLL slides (CD19, CD5, CD23 and dim CD20, without CD10) are the ones his objectives say you don't need. Follicular lymphoma Follicular lymphoma is a B-cell lymphoma that grows, at least in part, in a follicular pattern: crowded, back-to-back follicles fill the node. It makes up 10 to 20 percent of all lymphomas. The event that starts it is the translocation between chromosomes 14 and 18, t(14;18), found in 85 to 90 percent of cases. It moves the BCL2 gene next to the immunoglobulin heavy-chain gene, IGH, so BCL2 is switched on all the time (his slide: "constitutive expression of BCL2"). BCL2 blocks apoptosis, so the cells live on instead of dying. The neoplastic follicles stain for BCL2, which helps separate them from reactive follicles. Most patients already have widespread disease when it is found: nodes both near the surface and deep in the chest and abdomen, and an enlarged spleen; the marrow is involved in 40 to 70 percent. Yet patients are often asymptomatic, and B symptoms are uncommon. It is indolent: the median survival is more than 17 years with current treatment. But it keeps progressing over time, with no plateau in the survival curves, and the prognosis is closely tied to how far it had spread at diagnosis. Mantle cell lymphoma Mantle cell lymphoma is a mature B-cell lymphoma from the mantle zone of the lymphoid follicle, the rim of small B cells around the germinal center. Its cells are small to medium-sized, with slightly irregular nuclei and scant cytoplasm. Its genetic hallmark, and the first event in its development, is the translocation between chromosomes 11 and 14, t(11;14), present in at least 95 percent of cases. It switches on cyclin D1, and his slide calls the cyclin D1 stain diagnostic. Patients are older, with a median age of 68 to 69. Most present with enlarged peripheral lymph nodes, and the spleen and marrow are commonly involved. It used to be considered incurable; with current treatment the median survival has risen from 3 years to more than 5 to 10, and some patients may be cured. Marginal zone lymphoma and MALT lymphoma Marginal zone lymphoma comes in a nodal form and an extranodal one: extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue, called EMZL or MALT lymphoma. It is an indolent B-cell lymphoma that arises outside the nodes from marginal zone B cells, often on the ground of a chronic inflammatory disorder: long inflammation keeps lymphocytes dividing in a tissue, and in time a clone escapes. The common sites are the stomach, the ocular adnexa, the salivary glands, skin, lung, breast, thyroid and thymus. Patients have symptoms from a mass, or none at all and it is found by chance; B symptoms are rare. The associations are the testable part: Stomach Chronic Helicobacter pylori infection Skin (primary cutaneous) Borrelia burgdorferi Ocular adnexa Chlamydia psittaci Salivary gland Sjögren syndrome, which commonly comes first Thyroid Hashimoto thyroiditis, which commonly comes first Because infection drives some of these, a proportion respond to antibiotics. For the dentist, the salivary one matters: in a patient with Sjögren syndrome, a parotid that starts to enlarge should be checked for lymphoma. Under the microscope, atypical small to medium-sized lymphoid cells efface the tissue's architecture, often with lymphoepithelial lesions (tumor cells invading the gland's or the mucosa's epithelium). It is indolent: local recurrence, relapse in other MALT sites and spread to nodes can happen, but the overall survival is about 90 percent at 5 years and 80 percent at 10. Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is medium-sized to large B cells growing in a diffuse sheet. A cell counts as large when its nucleus is the size of a macrophage's nucleus or bigger, or more than twice the size of a small lymphocyte's nucleus. Compared with the low-grade B-cell lymphomas, the cells, the nuclei and the nucleoli are all bigger. It is the common one: about 30 percent of adult lymphomas. Most patients present with nodal disease, but 30 to 40 percent have disease only outside the nodes at diagnosis: the GI tract (stomach and ileocecal region), the head and neck (salivary glands, thyroid, ocular adnexa), bone, liver, kidney and adrenal gland. The typical story is a rapidly enlarging node or mass, at one site or several, with or without B symptoms. Its cause is unknown in most cases; risk factors include genetic features, immune dysregulation, and viral, environmental or occupational exposures. It can arise de novo or by transformation of an indolent B-cell lymphoma. After R-CHOP (rituximab with combination chemotherapy), the 5-year progression-free and overall survival are both about 70 percent. Burkitt lymphoma Burkitt lymphoma is a mature, aggressive B-cell lymphoma of medium-sized cells with basophilic (blue) cytoplasm and a very high proliferation index. Its cells double so fast that patients usually present with a high tumor burden, widespread disease and rapidly growing tumors, most often outside the nodes. Its primary genetic event is the translocation between chromosomes 8 and 14, t(8;14), in 80 percent of cases: it moves MYC, a gene that drives cell growth and division, next to the IGH locus. There are three clinical forms, and his objective names the first two. Endemic Equatorial Africa and Papua New Guinea, where it is the most common childhood cancer More than 90 percent Traditionally the mandible, maxilla and other facial bones; recent reports often describe the abdomen Sporadic Elsewhere in the world; less common in children About 20 percent Abdomen, orbit, Waldeyer ring, gingiva, thyroid, ovary, testis, breast Immunodeficiency-associated Most often with HIV Not on his slide Not on his slide The site symptoms matter in a dental school: altered vision, a blocked nose, enlarged tonsils, and dental or jaw pain, often with loss of teeth, along with abdominal masses (ileocecal lesions, retroperitoneal nodes), kidney lesions and testicular masses. His slide shows an endemic Burkitt tumor of the jaw. Under the microscope: sheets of uniform, medium-sized, cohesive blue cells, with many tingible-body macrophages scattered among them. These macrophages have eaten the debris of tumor cells that died by apoptosis, and their pale cytoplasm against the dark blue sheet gives the classic starry-sky pattern. With modern immunochemotherapy including rituximab, in high-resource settings, the prognosis is excellent: overall survival over 90 percent in children and 80 percent in adults. Classic Hodgkin lymphoma Classic Hodgkin lymphoma is different from the rest. The tumor cells are a small fraction of the mass, embedded in a reactive background rich in immune cells. They are the Hodgkin cells (one nucleus) and the Reed-Sternberg cells (two or more nuclei), together called HRS cells. The classic Reed-Sternberg cell has two nuclear lobes, each with a prominent, eosinophilic (pink) nucleolus, which gives it an owl's-eye look. They stain for CD30 in almost all cases and CD15 in most; his slide shows the CD30 stain, but the markers aren't needed. His slide's sentence about where it comes from is missing a word ("a neoplasm derived from characterized by"). The standard answer (Robbins, WHO) is that HRS cells come from germinal-center B cells. How it presents, and how that differs from non-Hodgkin lymphoma, is one of his objectives. Classic Hodgkin lymphoma mainly involves lymph nodes, with a striking preference for nodes above the diaphragm: more than 70 percent of patients with early-stage disease present with enlarged cervical or supraclavicular nodes, more than 60 percent have mediastinal involvement, and fewer than 5 percent have disease only below the diaphragm. The nodes are painless and firm, and the disease involves contiguous node groups, one to the next. Disease starting outside the nodes (skin, GI tract, Waldeyer ring, CNS) is rare. B symptoms appear in about 20 percent of localized and 70 percent of advanced disease. A rare but distinctive symptom: pain in the affected nodes after drinking alcohol. Its cause is unclear, but in EBV-positive cases there is strong evidence that latent EBV infection drives the malignant change. More than 80 percent are cured with modern combination chemotherapy, with radiotherapy for some. Nodular sclerosis Bands of fibrous (sclerotic) tissue surround nodules holding HRS cells and the reactive infiltrate Mixed cellularity The node is diffusely effaced; Reed-Sternberg cells are relatively frequent, in a mix of small lymphocytes, histiocytes, eosinophils and plasma cells; often EBV-associated Lymphocyte-rich Nodular or diffuse, with abundant small lymphocytes and virtually no neutrophils or eosinophils Lymphocyte-depleted Rare (2 percent or less); diffuse, with pleomorphic HRS cells; strongly associated with EBV His slide notes that subtyping may not matter for modern treatment. The non-Hodgkin lymphomas, by contrast, more often start outside the nodes (DLBCL 30 to 40 percent of the time, Burkitt mostly, MALT lymphoma by definition) and are often widespread at diagnosis. Plasma cell neoplasms Plasma cells are the antibody-making end of the B-cell line, so their tumors make monoclonal immunoglobulin. A plasmacytoma is a solitary tumor of clonal plasma cells. Patients present with pain, swelling or a fracture at that spot, or with spinal cord compression. The standard treatment of an extramedullary plasmacytoma is radiation to the involved field. Plasma cell myeloma is a bone marrow-based, multifocal proliferation of plasma cells. Multiple myeloma is plasma cell myeloma, usually with a monoclonal immunoglobulin in the serum or urine, plus either organ damage from the disease or, without it, lab or imaging findings that predict organ damage within 2 years. It is considered incurable for most patients. His slides show the findings: lytic bone lesions (punched-out holes in the bone on radiographs); an M-spike on protein electrophoresis, the monoclonal protein as one tall, narrow band; the CRAB features of organ damage, which stand for hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia and bone lesions; and rouleaux on the blood smear, red cells stacked like coins, because the large amount of immunoglobulin protein makes them stick together. In the jaw, myeloma's lytic lesions are radiolucencies and its calcium is high, so it can look like the brown tumors of hyperparathyroidism from Lecture A. The monoclonal protein, the rouleaux and the anemia point to myeloma. Peripheral T-cell lymphoma Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified (PTCL, NOS) is a mixed category: the mature T-cell lymphomas, in nodes or outside them, that don't fit a specific type. It is diagnosed nearly always in adults, and most present with advanced disease, usually lymphadenopathy and B symptoms, often with the marrow, liver, spleen, skin or GI tract involved. It carries T-cell markers, more often CD4 than CD8. These are aggressive lymphomas, with a poor response to therapy, frequent relapses and low survival. Mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome Mycosis fungoides is a T-cell lymphoma of the skin; with Sézary syndrome it is the most common type of cutaneous lymphoma, more than half of cases. Its lesions evolve in sequence: patches, then plaques, then tumors. They can be one or many; when localized they favor sun-protected skin, the flexures (armpits and groin) and the lower trunk and buttocks, a "bathing-trunk" distribution. Under the microscope, small to medium-sized T cells with a clear halo and hyperchromatic, hyperconvoluted ("cerebriform") nuclei line up along the basal layer and infiltrate the epidermis: they are epidermotropic. The course is indolent, over years or decades, with lesions that persist and grow slowly. It can appear at any age, peaking in the late fifties. Sézary syndrome is defined by a triad: erythroderma (red skin over most of the body), generalized lymphadenopathy, and clonal T cells with cerebriform nuclei, Sézary cells, in the skin, the lymph nodes and the peripheral blood. Unlike mycosis fungoides, it is aggressive: the 5-year survival is 10 to 30 percent, and most patients die of opportunistic infections. Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma is a lymphoma of NK-cell or T-cell lineage that damages and destroys blood vessels, with prominent necrosis, and a very strong association with EBV. It begins in the nasal cavity, nasopharynx, oropharynx, Waldeyer ring or epiglottis. From the nose it can grow out into the face or erode the nasal floor, destroying and perforating the hard palate, the picture once called "lethal midline granuloma". A dentist may be the first to see it. It occurs mainly in eastern Asia and among the Indigenous peoples of Central and South America, and is uncommon in Europe and the United States. The tumor grows diffusely around and into vessel walls (angiocentric and angiodestructive), commonly with coagulative necrosis. With chemotherapy and radiotherapy, the 5-year survival in early-stage disease is over 70 percent. Chronic myeloid leukemia Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm defined by the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene (the slides join the two names with a double colon), with too many neutrophils, a neutrophilic granulocytosis. At diagnosis, 90 to 95 percent carry the reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, t(9;22), which makes the shortened chromosome 22 called the Philadelphia chromosome. The fusion gene makes a tyrosine kinase that is always on. Its increased activity is necessary and sufficient to cause the chronic phase, by keeping several signaling pathways switched on. Its phases. In the chronic phase, the neoplastic cells stay mostly in the blood, marrow, spleen and liver. More than 95 percent are diagnosed in the chronic phase, which comes on insidiously; some patients have no symptoms and are found on a routine blood count. Untreated, most progress within a few years to an advanced phase: declining health, fever and weight loss, and worse anemia, low platelets, a rising white count and a growing spleen. In the blast phase, blasts can infiltrate any site outside the marrow, especially the spleen, liver, lymph nodes, skin and soft tissues. Its blood and marrow. The white count is high, from 12,000 to 1,000,000 per microliter, with a median of about 80,000 (the slide writes it as 12 to 1,000 times 10 to the 9th per liter). The cells are mostly neutrophils at every stage of maturation, with peaks at the myelocytes and the segmented neutrophils, not blasts. The marrow is hypercellular, more than 95 percent cellular, with granulocytes at every stage, and his slide shows small, hypolobated megakaryocytes. The karyotype shows the Philadelphia chromosome. Its treatment. Knowing the abnormal signal led to drugs that block it, the tyrosine kinase inhibitors, of which imatinib (Gleevec) was the first and is first-line therapy. It targets the enzymatically active part of the p210 BCR-ABL1 protein: it competes with ATP for the active site and so prevents the kinase from activating. In this era of kinase inhibitors, the most important sign of prognosis is the response to treatment, measured in the blood count, the chromosomes and the molecular test. Blasts and Auer rods Blasts are the hallmark of acute leukemia, but they are not found only there. In lower numbers, under 20 percent, they appear in other myeloid disorders that can come before AML, such as a myelodysplastic syndrome. And outside the newborn period, blasts in the peripheral blood are always abnormal. An Auer rod is a red-blue, needle-like inclusion in the cytoplasm of some myeloblasts, formed from abnormal granules that fuse. His slide adds that they are lysosomal and acid phosphatase-positive (textbooks also stress that they are myeloperoxidase-positive). An Auer rod marks the blast as myeloid, which is why Auer rods exclude ALL. Acute promyelocytic leukemia Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) is a type of AML in which abnormal promyelocytes predominate. Its genetic hallmark is a balanced translocation between chromosomes 15 and 17, t(15;17), which fuses the promyelocytic leukemia gene, PML, with the retinoic acid receptor alpha gene, RARA. The fusion protein, PML-RARA (written with a double colon on the slides), causes the disease by impairing myeloid differentiation: maturation stops at the promyelocyte. The cells look the part: abnormal promyelocytes whose cytoplasm is packed with large, dense granules staining bright pink, red or purple, and distinctive cells holding bundles of Auer rods scattered through the cytoplasm. On flow cytometry, their granules give a high side scatter (and they lack CD34 and HLA-DR, markers you don't need). The danger: APL is frequently associated with a coagulopathy and a risk of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), which can cause early death. In the mouth, that means bleeding gums, petechiae and bruising. The good news: all-trans retinoic acid with arsenic trioxide (ATRA plus ATO), without conventional chemotherapy, is highly effective and largely curative for low- and intermediate-risk APL. The retinoic acid lets the blocked promyelocytes mature. Acute monocytic leukemia and the gums Acute monocytic leukemia is an AML with monocytic differentiation and no defining genetic abnormality. The marrow is extensively infiltrated by immature, intermediate-sized to large cells with irregularly lobulated to kidney-shaped (reniform) nuclei, fine chromatin and distinct nucleoli. Flow cytometry shows two or more monocytic markers. Patients present with symptoms of their cytopenias, with disease outside the marrow, or both, and the oral cavity is one of those places. AML that forms a mass outside the marrow is called a myeloid sarcoma (extramedullary AML). In the mouth it shows as gingival hypertrophy: swollen gums infiltrated by leukemic cells. His slides cite two case reports, one of them a myeloid sarcoma of the mandibular gingiva that was the relapse of a treated AML. This is what his objective means by the extramedullary presentation of acute leukemia. Swollen gums in a patient who is tired, pale and bruising call for a blood count. B-lymphoblastic leukemia B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (B-ALL/LBL, also called precursor B-cell ALL) is a neoplasm of precursor lymphoid cells committed to the B-cell line. When it involves the marrow, and usually the blood, it is B-ALL; when nodes or other tissues are the primary sites, it is B-lymphoblastic lymphoma. It is diagnosed by morphology and flow cytometry (the blasts essentially always carry B-lineage antigens) and classified further by its cytogenetic and molecular abnormalities, which carry prognostic and treatment implications. No set blast number is required, although a diagnosis with under 20 percent blasts is made with caution. B-ALL occurs mainly in children: 75 percent of patients are under 6, and it is the most common leukemia of childhood. The incidence is bimodal, with a second, smaller peak in the fifth decade of life (the 40s). It usually presents with bone marrow failure: low platelets, anemia, low neutrophils, or all three. The lymphoblasts range from small cells with scant cytoplasm to larger ones with more pale blue-gray cytoplasm, sometimes vacuolated. With risk-stratified treatment, more than 90 percent of children reach long-term remission; adults do less well, because of harsher biology and the toxicity of treatment. T-lymphoblastic leukemia and lymphoma T-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma is the same idea in the T-cell line. It is called T-ALL when the blood and marrow are the primary sites and T-lymphoblastic lymphoma (T-LBL) when the primary site is a lymph node, the mediastinum (thymus) or another tissue such as the skin, tonsils, liver, spleen, CNS or testes. Again, no set blast number is required, with caution under 20 percent. T-ALL typically brings a high white count, often with a large mediastinal mass; lymphadenopathy and an enlarged liver and spleen are common. T-LBL often presents as a rapidly growing anterior mediastinal mass, sometimes as a respiratory emergency. Its lymphoblasts are indistinguishable under the microscope from those of B-ALL: flow cytometry, showing T-lineage antigens, tells them apart. Long-term response rates approach 85 percent in children and adolescents and 60 percent in adults. When acute leukemia comes from something else Acute leukemia, or a blast phase, can be the final stage of another marrow disorder, the result of treatment for a different cancer, or linked to a genetic disorder. Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS): persistent cytopenias with abnormal function and look of the red cell, granulocyte and/or megakaryocyte precursors. It may start with few blasts and progress to more. CML and CMML (chronic myelomonocytic leukemia). The myeloproliferative neoplasms, with persistently high counts: polycythemia vera (increased red cells), essential thrombocythemia (increased platelets) and primary myelofibrosis (fibrosis in the marrow). Myeloid neoplasm after cytotoxic therapy: after alkylating agents and/or ionizing radiation (type 1) or after topoisomerase II inhibitors (type 2). It generally arises within 10 years of the last exposure and has a bad prognosis. Myeloid proliferations of Down syndrome: two clonal conditions of children with trisomy 21, transient abnormal myelopoiesis and myeloid leukemia of Down syndrome. Treating acute leukemia Treatment of acute leukemia has two objectives: eradicate the leukemic cell mass, with cytoreductive chemotherapy, radiotherapy and marrow transplant, and provide supportive care. The goal is complete remission: no leukemia-related signs or symptoms, no demonstrable disease, and the return of marrow function, with the blood's granulocyte, platelet and red cell values back to normal. The translocations side by side Five translocations run through this lecture, and they are easy to swap. t(14;18) IGH and BCL2 Follicular lymphoma (85 to 90 percent) BCL2 always on, so the cells don't die t(11;14) Cyclin D1 and IGH Mantle cell lymphoma (at least 95 percent) Cyclin D1 on; the cyclin D1 stain is diagnostic t(8;14) MYC and IGH Burkitt lymphoma (80 percent) MYC on: very fast growth t(9;22) BCR and ABL1 (the Philadelphia chromosome) CML (90 to 95 percent) A tyrosine kinase always on; blocked by imatinib t(15;17) PML and RARA Acute promyelocytic leukemia Maturation stops at the promyelocyte; treated with retinoic acid and arsenic trioxide A memory hook: the three B-cell lymphomas all move a gene next to IGH on chromosome 14: BCL2 from 18 (follicular), cyclin D1 from 11 (mantle cell), MYC from 8 (Burkitt). The two myeloid ones are fusions: BCR with ABL1 in CML, PML with RARA in APL.
